author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 24, 2024 — original paper: https://mrbarton
summary: This page covers Siegfried Engelmann's evaluation of Project Follow Through, the largest educational experiment in U.S. history, which tested multiple instructional models on disadvantaged students. Direct Instruction (DI) consistently outperformed every other model on basic skills, cognitive skills, and affective measures, in some cases exceeding the performance of average students nationally. Barton's summary explains that the official evaluation was manipulated to downplay DI's effectiveness, and the wider educational establishment ultimately rejected the model in favor of approaches it found more ideologically congenial. The page argues that DI succeeded because of tightly designed content, moment-to-moment teacher-student interactions, and effective teacher training, not because of any special quality in the students themselves. It closes by framing this as a cautionary tale: proven, evidence-based practices can be suppressed by an educational system resistant to change.
points: Direct Instruction was the only model in Project Follow Through to consistently outperform other approaches across basic skills, cognitive skills, and affective measures, even besting average-student benchmarks.
DI's success held regardless of students' presumed learning styles, undermining the idea that instruction must be individually tailored to different learning preferences to be effective.
Teacher training matters as much as curriculum design: even previously struggling teachers reached high performance levels once trained in DI's structured approach.

The evaluation's results were manipulated and DI was ultimately rejected by the educational establishment, illustrating how ideology and politics can override evidence in shaping which practices get adopted.
quotes: This document details the Direct Instruction model, a program designed to improve the academic performance of disadvantaged students, and its surprising success in the Follow Through project.
Despite the program's strong results, the evaluation was manipulated to downplay its effectiveness, and the educational establishment ultimately rejected the Direct Instruction model.
The most important implication is that long-term, positive results are achievable for at-risk children from diverse backgrounds and settings through effective instruction.
The consistent success of DI across different types of learners debunks the myth that children need different approaches based on their learning styles.
DI's success across various sites suggests that even teachers who had previously struggled were able to achieve high levels of performance with the program.
Despite the undeniable success of DI, it faced resistance and rejection from the educational establishment, which favored less effective but more popular approaches.
